guide.title: Farmington, Connecticut: Grand Central Station of the Underground Railroad
guide.intro: Farmington was settled in June 1640 by English colonists from Hartford on land the Tunxis people called Tunxis Sepus, or "bend of the little river"; the town and river took their present name at incorporation in December 1645. The Farmington Canal, linking New Haven and Northampton, Massachusetts, operated along the river's eastern bank from 1828 to 1848, and its corridor is now a recreational rail-trail. In the 1800s, Farmington became known as the "Grand Central Station" of Connecticut's Underground Railroad. After the 1841 Amistad trial, 38 Mende Africans and Cinqué, leader of the shipboard revolt, were housed and educated in Farmington while residents raised funds for their return to Africa; First Church of Christ, Congregational, established in 1652, commemorates the connection in its Amistad Hall. Educational reformer Sarah Porter founded Miss Porter's School, the girls' preparatory school whose alumnae include Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, in the village center in 1843.

sections.heading: Tunxis Sepus to the Underground Railroad
sections.body: Farmington was settled in June 1640 by English colonists from Hartford on land the Tunxis people called Tunxis Sepus, 'bend of the little river'; the town and river took their present name at incorporation in December 1645. The Farmington Canal operated along the river's eastern bank from 1828 to 1848, linking New Haven with Northampton, Massachusetts, and its corridor is now the 81-mile Farmington Canal Heritage Trail. In the 1800s, Farmington became known as the 'Grand Central Station' of Connecticut's Underground Railroad, and after the 1841 Amistad trial, 38 Mende Africans and Cinqué, leader of the shipboard revolt, were housed and educated in town while residents raised funds for their return to Africa — a history First Church of Christ, Congregational commemorates in its Amistad Hall, and the Farmington Historical Society retraces on its Amistad walking tour. Sarah Porter founded Miss Porter's School, whose alumnae include Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, in the village center in 1843.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Farmington is a drive-to destination on Interstate 84, about 10 miles west of Hartford, reached via I-84's Farmington interchanges and state Routes 4, 10, and 177, plus US Route 6. There is no train station in town, so rail travelers take Amtrak or the CTrail Hartford Line to Hartford Union Station and drive or cab the last stretch.

sections.heading: Hill-Stead, the Canal Trail, and dinner on the Avenue
sections.body: Hill-Stead Museum, a 1901 Colonial Revival mansion designed by pioneering architect Theodate Pope Riddle, hangs Impressionist paintings by Monet, Degas, Manet, Whistler, and Cassatt across 152 hilltop acres, with a Beatrix Farrand sunken garden that hosts the summer-long Sunken Garden Poetry Festival. The circa-1720 Stanley-Whitman House, a National Historic Landmark near the village center, interprets early colonial life with period gardens and an orchard. For food, Piccolo Arancio and Victoria's Café sit beside the Farmington Inn on Farmington Avenue, with Wood-n-Tap Bar & Grill down the road for craft beer and weekly specials; the Farmington Inn & Suites itself, near the junction of Routes 4 and 10, is the village's boutique hotel.

faq.question: How do I get to Farmington?
faq.answer: Farmington sits on I-84 about 10 miles west of Hartford, via the Farmington interchanges and state Routes 4, 10, and 177. There's no train station in town; rail travelers use Amtrak or the CTrail Hartford Line to Hartford Union Station.

faq.question: What is Hill-Stead Museum?
faq.answer: A 1901 Colonial Revival mansion designed by Theodate Pope Riddle, with Impressionist paintings by Monet, Degas, Manet, Whistler, and Cassatt on 152 acres, plus a Beatrix Farrand sunken garden. Open Wednesday-Sunday 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

faq.question: What is Farmington's Amistad connection?
faq.answer: After the 1841 Amistad trial, 38 Mende Africans and Cinqué were housed and educated in Farmington while residents raised funds for their return to Africa. First Church of Christ, Congregational and the Farmington Historical Society's walking tour both commemorate the history.

faq.question: What is Miss Porter's School?
faq.answer: A girls' preparatory school founded in the village center in 1843 by educational reformer Sarah Porter; alumnae include Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.

faq.question: Where can I eat and stay in Farmington?
faq.answer: Piccolo Arancio is a longtime Italian bistro next to the Farmington Inn & Suites, with Wood-n-Tap Bar & Grill for craft beer down Farmington Avenue. The Farmington Inn & Suites, near Routes 4 and 10, is the village's boutique hotel, with Victoria's Café serving guests breakfast on site.

places.name: Hill-Stead Museum
places.summary: A 1901 Colonial Revival mansion on 152 hilltop acres designed by pioneering female architect Theodate Pope Riddle, hung with Impressionist paintings by Monet, Degas, Manet, Whistler, and Cassatt; its circa-1920 Beatrix Farrand sunken garden hosts the summer-long Sunken Garden Poetry Festival. Open Wednesday-Sunday 10 a.m.-4 p.m.; grounds daily 7:30 a.m.-5:30 p.m.; adult admission $20.

places.name: Stanley-Whitman House
places.summary: A living-history museum centered on a circa-1720 National Historic Landmark house furnished with period antiques, with gardens and an orchard interpreting early Connecticut colonial life. Open Wednesday-Saturday noon-4 p.m.; adult admission $14; tours run about 45 minutes.

places.name: Farmington Canal Heritage Trail
places.summary: An 81-mile rail-to-trail greenway following the 1828-1848 Farmington Canal corridor from New Haven to the Massachusetts border, linking with the 18-mile Farmington River Trail; maintained jointly by the Farmington Valley Trails Council and the Farmington Canal Rail-to-Trail Association.

photos.description: The riverside Farmington River Trail at Unionville, which links to the Farmington Canal Heritage Trail.

places.name: First Church of Christ, Congregational (1652)
places.summary: Established in 1652, this historic meetinghouse congregation is tied to Farmington's Amistad story — its Amistad Hall commemorates the Mende Africans sheltered in town in 1841. Sunday services at 10 a.m.

places.name: Farmington Historical Society — Amistad Walking Tour & Old Stone Schoolhouse
places.summary: Runs the 'Odyssey of the Amistad: A Trail to Freedom' walking tour of Farmington's Underground Railroad and Amistad sites, plus tours of the historic Old Stone Schoolhouse.

places.name: Piccolo Arancio
places.summary: Family-run classic Italian bistro next door to the Farmington Inn; a five-time Wine Spectator 'Award of Excellence' winner. Hours Mon-Thu 4-9 p.m., Fri-Sat 4-9:30 p.m.

places.name: Wood-n-Tap Bar & Grill (Farmington)
places.summary: Farmington outpost of the Connecticut-grown tap-and-grill group, known for its large craft beer selection and weekly specials. Hours Sun-Thu 11 a.m.-10:30 p.m., Fri-Sat to 11 p.m.

places.name: Victoria's Café (at The Farmington Inn)
places.summary: The Farmington Inn's complimentary guest-breakfast café — waffles, pastries, fruit, and coffee for hotel guests. It does not publish standalone hours or a menu for non-guests.

places.name: The Farmington Inn & Suites
places.address: 827 Farmington Avenue (junction of Routes 4 & 10), Farmington, CT 06032
places.summary: Boutique inn near Farmington's historic Main Street with suites and a guest house, marble bathrooms, Victoria's Café on site, and Piccolo Arancio next door; hosts weddings and meetings.
